canonical_question: How was the 'large tensile ductility (~20%)' measured at the high temperature of 800 K, and does it represent room temperature or elevated temperature behavior?

question_variants.question: How was the 'large tensile ductility (~20%)' measured at the high temperature of 800 K, and does it represent room temperature or elevated temperature behavior?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text states the alloys have large tensile ductility (~20%) and are workable at high temperatures (peak damping at nearly 800 K). It implies these mechanical properties are associated with the high-temperature performance, though the specific tensile test temperature for the 20% elongation is not explicitly isolated from the high-temperature context in the summary spans provided.

answers.answer: The text reports large tensile ductility (~20%) in the context of 'mechanically strong and workable at high temperatures' with a peak damping capacity at nearly 800 K. This suggests the 20% elongation represents elevated temperature behavior.
answers.material: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEAs blended with O or N
answers.processing_state: blended with 2.0 atomic % O or N
answers.mechanism: High-damping HEAs show a good combination of high-temperature damping capacity and excellent mechanical properties
answers.boundary_limitation: Specific test temperature for the 20% ductility is grouped with high-temperature performance
evidence_spans: Here, we report about a previously undiscovered class of high-damping alloys that are both mechanically strong and workable at high temperatures. The current alloy design concept has been realized in the form of a set of model Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEAs blended with 2.0 atomic % (at %) oxygen or nitrogen, respectively. These high-damping HEAs show a good combination of high-temperature damping capacity, i.e., their peak damping capacity is as high as ~0.030 at a peak temperature of nearly 800 K, along with excellent mechanical properties (tensile yield strength, ~1400 MPa; elongation, ~20%).

source_evidence_spans: The here designed HEAs also have large tensile ductility (~20%).
